title: Tibetan Empire
capsule: The Tibetan Empire was established by Songtsen Gampo (r. c. 617–649), who unified the Yarlung Plateau, introduced a written script for Tibetan, and forged alliances through marriage with both the Tang court of China and the Nepali Licchavi dynasty. Under Trisong Detsen (r. 755–797) the empire reached its maximum extent, seizing the Tang capital Chang'an briefly in 763 and controlling territories from the Pamirs and Tarim Basin to the borders of Bengal; the Tang were forced to acknowledge Tibetan supremacy in the Treaty of 783. Fragmenting power struggles among regional nobles and Buddhist monastic factions led to the assassination of the anti-Buddhist king Langdarma in 842, after which the central authority collapsed and the empire dissolved into competing principalities by the mid-ninth century.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Tibetan imperial boundaries are partially attested by Chinese annals (Old and New Tang Shu), Tibetan royal inscriptions at Zhol and Skar-cung, and Dunhuang documents; frontier zones in the Tarim Basin and toward Bengal are reconstructed conjecturally from campaign records.
